projects.heading: Birthday Site
projects.html: From late April to mid May of 2025 I designed and created a website to convince my family to get me a Mac Mini. I was inspired by Beno Grids and Nev Flynn's Dev Site. I made my site on an old all-in-one computer. My site featured a four wide grid I used to showcase reasons I wanted my Mac Mini. Each box was a very basic div: rounded corners and a black border. To adapt to smaller screens, I added basic CSS responive web design (RWD) to shrink boxes down and cut the gride width. This was my first time using RWD and it shows. Much of the shrinking is messy and breaks some parts of the site.

projects.heading: Capybraita
projects.html: Capybraita is a game two others and I made for a Hackathon in Bogotá, Colombia. The game was made in Unity over three days. In Capybraita, you play as a broke capybara trying to save up for a computer. You complete minigames around a Colombian neighborhood to earn mangoes, the game's currency. However, to stay alive, you must eat mangoes. The game wasn't great, we had a lot of bumps in the road. However we did ship it, and we definitely followed the hackathon theme: "make something ridiculous."

projects.heading: Isaac The Carpentopod
projects.html: Isaac The Carpentopod is a walking robot that uses 3D printed legs powered by DC moters. A special ration of leg lengths: Giliam de Carpentier's Carpentopod Linkage. Isaac's body is fully 3D printed in PLA, his brain is an Arduinio mega paired with an L298N dual motor driver that powers both of Isaac's Gearbox DC Motors. These rations were generated by Giliam using software that eveloved thousands of leg generations until it found an ideal linkage. Giliam was inspried by Jansen's linkage, a similar linkage designed by kinetic sculptor Theo Jansen for his Strandbeest.

projects.heading: Just The Info
projects.html: Just The Info was my attempt at summarizing news via AI. The project had a Python backend that pulled stories from CNN Lite and used Gemini 2.5 Flash to summarize these stories. I then updated a pretty boring HTML page via JavaScript. The project had various flaws, the biggest being my lack of JS experience at the time. I also had to conserve Gemini usage to 10 or so daily stories. I also struggled with creating a GitHub action to auto-run the Python file. I definitely learned a lot from the project, but I never produced anything amazing.

projects.heading: Mac And Cheese-Ropad
projects.html: Mac And Cheese-Ropad is a macropad I designed for Hack Club Blueprint. The macropad was designed to have 16 switches in a 4x4 layout. I used KiCad to design the PCB, Onshape for the case, and QMK for the firmware. Because I was new to macropads, I followed a Hack Club guide that helped me learn KiCad. After some design iteration I submitted my project and Hack Club sent me the PCB and parts I needed. Currently the macropad is soldered but has some hardware issues.

projects.heading: WXTUI
projects.html: WxTUI is a free, open source terminal user interface that uses National Weather Service (NWS) data to bring up live alerts/warnings. Displaying this information using Textual. WxTUI allows users to customize what alerts they see. I built WxTUI for Hackclub Macondo. WxTUI is entirly python, using the Textual library to display information. I am planing a version 2 of WxTUI that will add increased weather forecasting and tropical system tracking.

blogs.heading: Macondo Hackathon
blogs.subheading: From August 14-16, I attended a Hack Club hackathon in Bogotá, Colombia.
blogs.lead: Hackathon! This was the word that drew me to Hack Club's Macondo program in the first place. I really wanted to go. Even though I had never been to a hackathon and never really knew about them, I was determined to go.
blogs.html: Hackathon! This was the word that drew me to Hack Club's Macondo program in the first place. I really wanted to go. Even though I had never been to a hackathon and never really knew about them, I was determined to go. I had the opportunity to spend the 13th in Bogotá, experiencing the amazing vibe of the city. I tried amazing foods and also got to work on this very website. The hackathon itself was a blast and a blur. It started rough when I got teamed up with two Spanish speakers; we agreed that it would be best if I joined a new team. My new team also made me unsure of myself. They were both older and more experienced than me. They also wanted to develop a game, something I didn't really know much about. After some brainstorming, I felt more prepared but went to bed nervous. Day 2 was a real turning point. We made excellent progress on our game and bonded more (I mean, it's hard not to when you're spending hours in a cubicle). I felt a lot more useful; I was understanding Unity more and feeling more confident in myself. Even though the progress we made was great, the game still needed much more development before it could become what we really wanted. Later in the day, we went to Monserrate, a beautiful mountain that overlooks all of Bogotá. We took cable cars up and a funicular down. Day 3, the final day, was really stressful. We were up late into the early morning, so we slept in. We began work at around 9 AM, with only two and a half hours until projects were due. Every change sparked a billion more issues that we had to clean up. In the end, our game worked, but it was lacking a lot of features we wanted. My teammates had to leave very early to catch their flight, leaving me with an issue: the game had a bug. Essentially, the button to start the minigame didn't call the correct function. Through some help from the amazing organizers and my teammates on Slack, I got the game working in time for the presentation! Although we didn't win any awards, the environment, experience, and project gave me a new love for hackathons. Hack Club Macondo
